645.bp: Large language models now drive everything from customer support to content moderation, but they only work when their outputs match what people actually want. To make them safe and useful, companies use human feedback to steer the model toward good behavior—the foundational technique behind modern AI assistants.
645.wh: Labeling what counts as 'good' output is inherently subjective and error-prone. About one in four training examples in real preference datasets contradict themselves: a reward model (a separate AI judge trained on feedback) rates one answer better, but the human who labeled it picked the opposite. Training on these conflicting signals teaches the main model wrong lessons, actually making it worse instead of better.

The paper finds that roughly 25% of preference pairs show clear inconsistencies—the reward model's judgment conflicts with the human label. When you train on such contradictions, the model learns to chase both goals at once, which leaves it confused and under-aligned.
645.ap: AlignCP assigns a confidence score to each training example based on how strongly the reward model agrees with itself, and a polarity score based on whether the reward model's ranking matches the original human label. Examples with high confidence and matching polarity get full weight; low-confidence or mismatched examples get downweighted or dropped entirely. The framework automates all of this without asking humans to re-label.
645.ww: By trusting examples the reward model already approves of and ignoring the contradictory ones, the learning signal becomes cleaner. The model trains on a curated set of examples that all point in the same direction, like focusing a camera lens on a clear image instead of an out-of-focus one.
645.po: The paper shows this noise-aware reweighting improves model alignment on standard benchmarks—the model generates outputs that better match human preferences. Since preference quality is the bottleneck in deploying safe language models, this directly improves real-world safety and usefulness at scale.

646.bp: Networks of connected entities—social networks, computer systems, sensor arrays—contain both normal nodes that behave like their neighbors and anomalies that stand out. Detecting these anomalies (fraud, system failures, intrusions) is critical, but it's expensive to scan huge graphs and hard when the notion of 'normal' changes from one node or category to another.
646.wh: Most graph anomaly detection assumes all nodes follow the same pattern: normal nodes cluster with similar neighbors, anomalies break that pattern. But in reality, some nodes naturally sit in homogeneous neighborhoods (like a bank teller surrounded by other bank employees) while others sit in diverse ones (like a tourist in many countries). A fixed approach that assumes one pattern misses anomalies in the diverse case and flags false alarms in the homogeneous one.
646.ap: SAGAD precomputes embeddings that capture both low-frequency patterns (what its neighbors look like) and high-frequency patterns (unique properties of this node). It then uses a fusion mechanism that adapts per-node, deciding whether to trust the neighborhood similarity signal or the node's own distinct features based on the node's local structure. A separate loss guides anomalies to retain more of their unique high-frequency information than normal nodes do.
646.ww: Anomalies often hide in diverse neighborhoods or have unusual features that don't match their surroundings. By letting the system adaptively choose between neighborhood-based and feature-based signals for each node, and by encouraging anomalies to preserve their unusual features, the method respects that 'deviant' can mean different things in different parts of the graph.
646.po: The paper reports that SAGAD detects anomalies across multiple benchmark graphs while using far less memory and compute than prior methods—linear time and space complexity. This scalability matters because real graphs have millions or billions of nodes, and the per-node adaptivity catches anomalies that fixed-threshold methods miss.

647.bp: Converting English questions into SQL queries is how millions of people query databases every day without writing code. Large language models have gotten quite good at this, but the SQL they generate often breaks: it might have a typo, misunderstand the table structure, or silently compute the wrong result. Catching and explaining these errors before they reach users is essential.
647.wh: Existing error detection methods are slow (they require human review or expensive AI model calls) and they don't explain what went wrong. When a model says 'this SQL is broken,' it doesn't tell you whether it's a syntax error, a logic flaw, or a schema mismatch—so a user can't fix it. The real challenge is generating high-quality training data for an error detector, because manually labeling all the ways SQL can fail is prohibitively expensive.
647.ap: SQL-Checker first catalogs the common error types (like table mismatch, join mistake, aggregation error). It then uses a data synthesis pipeline: start with a base SQL statement, inject one of these known errors, and ask a large language model to analyze the error in detail. For complex cases, it refines the analysis iteratively, asking the model to critique its own earlier explanation. This creates a dataset of errors paired with interpretable labels describing the root cause.
647.ww: By simulating realistic errors methodically and having the language model explain each one, the training data covers the error space in a structured way—far better than random coverage. The model learns to recognize both that an error exists and what kind of error it is, building genuine understanding rather than just pattern matching.
647.po: The paper shows SQL-Checker achieves state-of-the-art error detection on multiple benchmarks and, when added to an existing text-to-SQL pipeline, improves the execution accuracy of SQL queries. Users and downstream systems see fewer broken queries and when an error is flagged, they get a meaningful explanation of what failed.

648.bp: Graphs—networks of connected data like social networks or knowledge bases—are intellectual property and need protection. When someone creates a valuable knowledge graph or social network, they need a way to prove they own it and detect if someone has stolen or tampered with it, much like a watermark on a document.
648.wh: Watermarking a graph is much harder than watermarking an image or document. You can't just hide a bit pattern in the structure because modifying the watermark slightly risks destroying the whole graph's utility. Also, hidden messages in graph structure get tangled up with the actual relationships the graph represents, making it hard to extract the watermark without corrupting the data.
648.ap: DRGW learns separate representations: one captures the structural topology (how nodes connect) and another holds the watermark (the proof of ownership). It uses an adversarially trained encoder that stays stable even when the graph gets perturbed, and an invertible neural network that can embed and extract the watermark without losing information. A structure-aware editor translates the watermark back into actual graph modifications, so the embedded watermark survives realistic changes to the graph.
648.ww: By separating structure from watermark signal, each can be optimized independently. The structural representation stays robust to damage because it's trained against adversarial perturbations. The invertible network guarantees no information loss during embedding, so the watermark always comes back cleanly. This separation is the key: you can protect ownership without entangling it with the graph's actual meaning.
648.po: The paper demonstrates that DRGW's watermarks survive structural attacks (node deletions, edge flips) and remain extractable, while preserving the original graph's utility. This enables graph datasets to be published or shared with cryptographic proof of provenance—critical for protecting research and industrial knowledge graphs.

649.bp: People share personal information constantly: health data on fitness apps, location on maps, shopping history on social media. Each individual disclosure seems low-risk, but an adversary who watches across time and combines fragments from many sources builds an increasingly accurate profile. The real privacy risk is cumulative, not instantaneous.
649.wh: Most privacy models treat each disclosure as independent—lock down one thing and you're done. But they miss the aggregation threat: an adversary can piece together information over weeks or months. Also, both the user and the adversary learn and adapt: if a user sees their data was misused, they share less next time; if an adversary realizes the user is guarding something, they try a different angle. These dynamics are hard to model with standard game theory.
649.ap: The paper formulates continual information sharing as a dynamic Stackelberg game (a sequential game where the user decides first, then the adversary responds, then the user adapts, and so on). The user's goal is to balance sharing enough data to get utility (like personalized recommendations) while keeping cumulative exposure low. The game captures both players' beliefs about what the other will do next, and both adapt their strategies over time.
649.ww: By modeling it as a sequential game with learning, the framework captures the real interplay: users rationally reveal less if they see patterns of misuse, and adversaries rationally focus on gathering info over time rather than one big exploit. This matches how privacy actually works in practice—as a dynamic negotiation, not a one-shot decision.
649.po: The paper presents a reinforcement learning algorithm that computes approximately optimal sharing strategies for users, and demonstrates on real-world datasets that following these strategies significantly reduces the cumulative privacy risk compared to static or reactive approaches.

650.bp: Social networks and collaborator graphs often store edge weights: how frequently two people interact, or how strongly they're connected. These weights should help partition the network into communities, but they also come with noise and storage costs. A smart clustering should clean up the noise and only store weights that actually matter.
650.wh: Edge weights can mean very different things in different parts of the graph, and they introduce noise—a weight might be inflated by a one-time spike or an artifact of how the data was collected. If you just add raw weights to a clustering algorithm, you risk either blowing up memory usage on large graphs or letting noisy edges mislead the clustering. Few methods jointly optimize both the clustering and the edge weights themselves.
650.ap: The paper proposes a graph contraction module that removes less important nodes while preserving the structural information needed for clustering (like key hub nodes), reducing the graph size. It then learns an attention weight for each edge that scales down noisy connections. An edge-weight-aware network fuses this cleaned-up information to find clusters, and a special loss encourages this process by making anomalies (noise-prone edges) carry less weight.
650.ww: Shrinking the graph first reduces noise exposure and memory use. By learning which edges are noisy and downweighting them adaptively, the clustering algorithm works with a cleaner signal. The joint optimization means edge weights improve specifically for the clustering task, not for some generic reconstruction objective.
650.po: The paper shows on real weighted graphs that this approach outperforms baselines at finding tight, meaningful clusters, while also reducing memory footprint and training time—practical benefits for clustering large social networks or collaboration graphs.

651.bp: Mapping services like Baidu Maps or Google Maps answer millions of queries every day: 'Find me a restaurant near the train station' or 'Show me the hospital hours.' Large language models can understand these queries, but they only work well when connected to the right data sources (APIs)—like a restaurant database or a hospital directory—and knowing which API to call requires manual engineering.
651.wh: As user queries diversify, the set of APIs needed grows constantly. Manually discovering which new APIs solve which kinds of questions, then writing the code to call them and training the AI model to use them, is slow and expensive. Automating this requires both understanding what the user actually wants (extracting the intent) and finding or designing the right API for it—two hard problems in tandem.
651.ap: ARADD uses a multi-stage pipeline: first, a language model and a lightweight agent work together to extract each new user intent (what the person really needs). Second, the system identifies existing APIs that could serve that intent, or designs new ones. Third, it generates training examples (question-answer pairs) automatically by having the model explain how to use each API. A self-guided refinement loop polishes the low-quality examples.
651.ww: By having the model generate its own explanations of how APIs work, and then filtering out the explanations it's uncertain about, the system bootstraps training data without human labelers. Iterative refinement catches errors the model made in earlier rounds. The intent-extraction stage ensures you're solving the real user need, not just surface-level keywords.
651.po: The paper describes ARADD deployed at Baidu (a real-world service), discovering new APIs from user queries and integrating them into the AI Guide service. This automation reduces manual labor and biases in API selection, letting the system scale to handle diverse user intents.

652.bp: Biomedical researchers use meta-analyses to synthesize evidence from hundreds of papers on a treatment or disease. They manually read each paper's full text to extract key details: what population was studied, what intervention was tested, what outcomes were measured (PIO elements). This screening process is the bottleneck—with thousands of new papers published monthly, it's impossible to keep up.
652.wh: Automating this with simpler methods (binary classifiers that just filter papers) still requires human review of thousands of results. Summarization models often hallucinate or omit details, because they're trained on general text, not on medical papers where precision is critical. The challenge is extracting structured PIO elements accurately while scaling to handle large volumes.
652.ap: The pipeline segments PDF papers into semantic chunks (using XML structure), then feeds these to a large language model with adaptive prompting: complex chunks get detailed, multi-step prompts; simple ones get direct prompts. The model generates multiple candidate summaries of the PIO elements, then a consensus filter (looking for agreement across candidates) produces a single high-confidence summary.
652.ww: By breaking the paper into semantic units first, the model processes manageable pieces rather than overwhelming context. Adaptive prompting matches the prompting strategy to the difficulty—don't over-engineer simple passages. The consensus filter acts like human review but automatically: if multiple independent model runs agree, the output is likely right; if they disagree, the filter can flag it for human review.
652.po: The paper shows an 8-billion-parameter model with this pipeline achieves semantic precision above 0.88 and recall above 0.91 on the EBM-NLP benchmark, matching much larger models. Human expert review confirms the extracted PIO elements are factually accurate, making this practical for accelerating meta-analysis screening.

653.bp: Banks and financial institutions collect detailed transaction and customer data, but strict privacy regulations (like GDPR) limit how they can share or analyze it. Synthetic data—artificially generated datasets that preserve statistical patterns without revealing real individuals—is a potential solution. But synthetic financial data is hard: transactions are rare events (most customers aren't committing fraud), attributes are mixed (categorical account type, continuous transaction amount), and the privacy guarantees are unclear.
653.wh: Existing synthetic data generators (like GANs or autoencoders) were designed for balanced, homogeneous datasets. Financial data violates both: it has severe class imbalance (99%+ normal transactions) and mixed data types. Standard generators either fail on imbalanced data or create synthetic datasets that preserve utility poorly. And if you want formal privacy guarantees, you must adapt the generator implementation—but few papers study whether that adaptation even works in the financial domain.
653.ap: The paper compares several generator architectures (autoencoders, GANs, diffusion models, copula methods) on financial datasets, and proposes privacy-preserving versions of GAN and autoencoder generators. It evaluates each on three dimensions: data quality (does synthetic data look like real data?), downstream task utility (can you train a classifier on synthetic data and use it on real data?), and privacy (how close is the synthetic data to the real data?).
653.ww: By comparing multiple generators and measuring quality/utility/privacy together, the paper shows which trade-offs are unavoidable and which aren't. Privacy-preserving implementations (like differential privacy) usually hurt utility, so understanding the exact trade-off curve is essential for choosing a generator for a specific use case.
653.po: The paper provides empirical guidance on which generators work best for financial data given different privacy-utility preferences. This helps financial institutions decide whether synthetic data can safely replace or augment real data for analysis, a critical decision given regulatory constraints.

654.bp: Graph foundation models are neural networks trained on massive graphs (billions of nodes and edges) to learn general-purpose representations that transfer to new tasks. They're the graph equivalent of models like BERT for text. But they try to compress the entire knowledge of a huge graph into model parameters—which is like memorizing an encyclopedia inside your brain instead of using a library.
654.wh: Compressing all graph knowledge into parameters creates three problems: there's simply not enough capacity for large graphs (semantic loss), different parts of the graph have conflicting patterns (parameter conflicts), and when you want to adapt the model to a new task or graph, the compressed knowledge is tangled up with the task-specific learning, making adaptation harder.
654.ap: RAG-GFM separates the compressed knowledge (what stays in the model) from the full knowledge (stored in retrieval databases). It builds two external stores: a semantic store of text descriptions of nodes and relationships, and a structural store of important subgraph patterns (motifs). When the model processes a graph, it retrieves relevant text and motifs from these stores as context, using a dual-view loss that makes sure both the semantic and structural retrieved information align with the task.
654.ww: By keeping the full graph knowledge external, the model can learn task-specific patterns without lossy compression. Retrieval gives it access to all the graph information it needs without storing it in parameters. The model learns what to retrieve (routing) and how much to retrieve (depth), making adaptation more flexible and interpretable—you can see what graph context it used for each decision.
654.po: The paper shows RAG-GFM outperforms 13 prior models on node and graph classification tasks across five benchmarks. The external knowledge store also improves interpretability—you can explain model decisions by pointing to the retrieved context—and enables more efficient domain adaptation to new graphs.

655.bp: Multimodal sentiment analysis reads text, looks at images, and hears audio in videos to understand emotion and opinion. A sarcastic tweet ('I *love* waiting in traffic') needs both the text and visual context (e.g., a frustrated emoji or gesture) to get the sentiment right. This is how humans understand nuance, and it's how systems should too.
655.wh: Most methods extract features from each mode (text, image, audio) separately and then combine them. But this misses fine-grained, local cross-modal interactions: a specific word paired with a specific gesture carries sentiment that neither the word nor the gesture alone can convey. Existing global fusion approaches smooth over these fine details, and aligning information across modes without losing local richness is technically hard.
655.ap: CCAF builds two alignment and fusion pathways: a coarse-grained one that aligns and fuses global patterns (overall sentiment of the post), and a fine-grained one that aligns and fuses local cross-modal interactions (word-gesture pairs, specific facial expressions tied to words). It uses optimal transport to align information across modalities at both levels, gated attention to fuse the aligned signals, and learnable sentiment prototypes to filter out redundant information at each level.
655.ww: By explicitly capturing both global and local cross-modal signals, the method doesn't lose nuance. Optimal transport respects the geometry of how different modalities relate (semantic distance between text features and visual features), so alignment is meaningful, not arbitrary. The prototype-based filtering learns what sentiment information matters and what's noise.
655.po: The paper reports that CCAF achieves superior results on two multimodal sentiment datasets, capturing sarcasm and nuanced emotion better than prior coarse-only or local-only methods. This improves sentiment analysis on social media and video content where emotional nuance is everything.

656.bp: Search engines rank documents in response to a query, and we want to know: is this ranking good? The same question comes up in evaluating recommendation systems, LLM re-rankers, and answer generation. We use ground-truth labels (what are the truly relevant documents?) to measure how well a ranking performs—but our labels are almost never complete, and we need a metric that accounts for that uncertainty.
656.wh: A naive metric would give equal weight to every position in the ranking—but users almost never scroll past the first few results. Position 1 matters much more than position 100. We could use a fixed weight scheme (position 1 gets weight 1, position 2 gets weight 0.5, etc.), but then the scheme's choice becomes arbitrary. Also, if your ground truth labels are incomplete, a metric that assumes completeness will mislead you.
656.ap: Rank-biased measurement assigns weights to ranks using a geometric distribution: weight falls off geometrically as you go deeper in the ranking (position 1 gets full weight, position 2 gets 0.8×, position 3 gets 0.64×, etc., where the decay factor is a tunable parameter). This is mathematically principled: it sums to a finite total (unlike other schemes), and it models a plausible user browsing behavior (each position has a constant probability the user will look further).
656.ww: The geometric weighting both matches how users actually browse (they stop looking after a few results) and is mathematically elegant (finite sum, interpretable parameter). The bounded sum means you can meaningfully compare rankings of different lengths. The parameter lets you tune how much you care about top positions (set it high to focus on top-1, set it low to care more about deeper results).
656.po: The paper (presented as a keynote) reviews rank-biased precision and its variants, showing how to properly measure ranking quality in web search, information retrieval, and LLM re-ranking tasks, and how to account for incomplete ground truth. This theoretical foundation underpins modern search evaluation.

657.bp: Knowledge graphs store facts in a structured form: 'Albert Einstein studied_at University of Zurich,' where entities (Einstein, the university) are linked by relations (studied_at). Real-world knowledge graphs often have images, descriptions, or other media tied to entities. Learning numeric vectors (embeddings) that represent these entities and relations is fundamental to knowledge graph reasoning, but adding image and text data makes it much harder.
657.wh: Standard embedding methods assume all entities have the same type of data or ignore modalities separately. A real knowledge graph might have an image for one artist but not for another, rich text for a company but minimal data for a person. Cross-modal alignment (making sure the image and text for the same entity point to the same latent concept) is needed, but it's hard to enforce when modalities are sparse or misaligned in content.
657.ap: VL-KGE combines vision-language models (pre-trained on pairs of images and text) with the structured reasoning of knowledge graphs. For each entity, it uses the VLM to align its available modalities (image and/or text) into a shared embedding space. The graph structure (which entities connect to which) is then learned alongside this multimodal alignment, ensuring that the final embeddings preserve both the cross-modal relationships and the graph structure.
657.ww: Vision-language models have already learned how images and text concepts relate to each other, so leveraging that pre-learned alignment is better than learning alignment from scratch on sparse graph data. By aligning modalities first and then learning graph structure, the entity embeddings capture both semantic meaning (from the media) and relational meaning (from the graph).
657.po: The paper shows VL-KGE improves link prediction (predicting missing facts) on standard benchmarks and on two new fine-art knowledge graphs. The multimodal embeddings are more robust and better transfer to downstream tasks than unimodal embeddings, making knowledge graphs with mixed media much more useful.

658.bp: Dialogue systems like ChatGPT need to remember long conversations: what the user asked 50 turns ago, preferences mentioned earlier, decisions made together. Without memory, each turn starts from scratch. With good long-term memory, the system can refer back, avoid repetition, and give personalized responses that feel continuous.
658.wh: Simple approaches (storing everything and searching it) are slow and wastes space on redundant details. Other methods (summarizing the history) lose important details and often hallucinate. The real problem is that users ask about different things—sometimes they want factual recall ('what restaurant did I mention?'), sometimes they want emotional continuity ('remember when I was frustrated?'), sometimes they want patterns ('I like spicy food'). A one-size-fits-all memory strategy fails.
658.ap: HingeMem uses event boundaries (moments where the topic, location, person, or time changes) to structure memory. When a boundary is crossed, the current event is 'written' to memory as a record tied to those four elements. At retrieval time, the system adapts: it estimates what type of information the current query needs, then routes to the relevant element-indexed records and decides how much to retrieve (shallow recall for simple questions, deep for complex ones).
658.ww: Boundaries reduce redundancy: you write once per event change, not after every turn. Element-based indexing (person, time, location, topic) lets you retrieve what's relevant without scanning the whole history. Adaptive routing respects that different queries need different amounts of memory—'who did I meet?' needs deep retrieval of person elements, while 'what time is it?' needs almost none.
658.po: The paper shows HingeMem achieves 20% better performance on the LOCOMO dialogue benchmark across models from 0.6B to production scale, while reducing computational cost by 68% compared to baselines. This makes long-context dialogues practical for resource-constrained settings.

659.bp: Real-world events don't happen at regular intervals: hospital patient vital signs change unpredictably, financial transactions cluster around payday, tweets spike when news breaks. Modeling these asynchronous sequences is crucial for healthcare, finance, social networks, and anomaly detection. The right model captures not just what events happen, but when and how they influence future events.
659.wh: Classical point process models (like Hawkes processes) assume parametric forms for how past events influence future ones (typically, exponential decay). This is too rigid for complex, real data. Modern neural approaches (RNNs, Transformers) are more flexible but computationally expensive: they need to scan all past events, creating quadratic complexity. Also, Transformers suffer from attention saturation—after seeing many events, the model struggles to attend to the most relevant ones.
659.ap: The paper introduces Mamba Hawkes Process (MHP), which combines Mamba (a recent state space model with linear complexity) with temporal point process theory. State space models maintain a hidden state that evolves over time, where each new event updates the state via an input-dependent gate. MHP adds time-aware mechanisms: the state transition rate adapts to the event type and history, and a separate mechanism scales time intervals to account for heterogeneous event dynamics.
659.ww: State space models achieve linear complexity by processing events sequentially without storing all pairwise interactions. Mamba's input-dependent gating naturally captures which past events matter (the 'selective' part), avoiding the attention saturation problem. By adding time-scaling and dual-channel state transitions, MHP respects that events in different domains (healthcare vs. finance) have different temporal patterns.
659.po: The paper shows MHP generalizes classical Hawkes processes (proving theoretical recovery of exponential-decay models) while also outperforming RNN and Transformer baselines on benchmark event sequences. The linear complexity enables practical forecasting on long, real-world event sequences.
